Reversal: eventually a show comes out where the lead lives in a studio, eats convenience-store dinners, and fights the landlord over sixty bucks. You quit after two episodes. Turns out you didn't want realism. You wanted company while complaining about the lack of it.

items.sourceNote: 追劇族依螢幕剩餘時間預判劇情節奏的普遍習慣，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
追劇追到一個境界，你就不看角色的臉了，你看右下角的時間。

那對情侶在吵架，你瞄一眼——還剩二十六分鐘。
你反而放鬆，因為你知道這裡吵完還會和好，甚至來得及再吵一次。

反派把刀舉起來，你再瞄一眼——只剩九十秒。
你一點都不緊張，因為九十秒不夠死一個角色，最多只夠他轉個頭。

男主角終於要說出那句話了，你瞄一眼——四十秒。
你嘆一口氣，往後靠回椅背：這集不會給你答案。

四十集看下來，你發現這部劇裡最誠實的角色，
不是主角，也不是配角，
是那條進度條。

它從來沒騙過你。
它只是沒忍心告訴你——
你把編劇的時間表讀得太熟，已經弄丟了被嚇一跳的能力。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個看劇會先確認剩幾分鐘、再決定要不要緊張的朋友；發現這件事的那天，你就再也回不去了
variations: 延伸版：更麻煩的是這招會外溢。進電影院你會算「還有半小時，這個伏筆一定得回收」；聽朋友講心事你會算「他講這麼久，結局大概不好笑」。你不知不覺替生活也裝了一條進度條。
反轉版：所以你偶爾會刻意全螢幕、把時間軸藏起來，假裝自己不知道還剩多久。你花錢請一部劇騙你，結果連騙你這件事都得你自己幫忙。

en.content:
Binge long enough and you stop watching faces. You watch the clock in the corner.

The couple is fighting. You glance down — 26 minutes left.
You relax, because you know they make up inside this episode, with room for one more fight first.

The villain raises the knife. Glance — 90 seconds.
Zero tension. Ninety seconds isn't enough to kill a character. It's barely enough for him to turn around.

The lead finally opens his mouth to say the thing. Glance — 40 seconds.
You sigh and lean back. This episode is not going to answer you.

Forty episodes in, you realize the most honest character in the show
isn't the hero and isn't the sidekick.
It's the progress bar.

It has never lied to you.
It just couldn't bring itself to tell you the rest —
you've learned the writers' schedule so well that you misplaced your ability to be surprised.
en.editorNote: For the friend who checks the time remaining before deciding how worried to be; once you notice this, you can't unsee it
variations: Extended: worse, it leaks. In a theater you think "half an hour left, that setup has to pay off." Listening to a friend vent you think "he's been going this long, the ending won't land." You quietly installed a progress bar on your life.
Reversal: so once in a while you go full screen on purpose and hide the timeline, pretending not to know how much is left. You pay a show to fool you, and now you have to help it do it.

items.sourceNote: 觀眾記得大量劇情細節卻叫不出劇名的常見情形，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
你剛用三個晚上追完一部四十集的劇。
你為它熬夜、為它哭過、還為它跟朋友爭執了一次。

隔天同事問你：「你最近在看什麼？」

你張開嘴，發現自己想不起劇名。

於是你開始比手畫腳：
「就那個……男主角是律師的那部。」
「不是那部，是有下雨那場的那部。」
「女主角短頭髮，後來搬去別的城市。」
「配樂超好聽，你一定聽過。」

同事一臉困惑，你越講越急，
最後你放棄了：「算了，我等等傳給你。」

你的記性沒有問題。
你記得那句台詞停頓在第幾個字、記得他哭的時候鏡頭在哪一邊，
你甚至記得看那集的時候自己坐在哪裡。

你只是從來沒有把它歸檔成「一部作品」。
它對你不是一個名字，
是那三個晚上，有人陪著你。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個永遠用「就那個誰演的那部」在推薦劇的朋友；記不住名字不代表它不重要，通常剛好相反
variations: 延伸版：後來你養成一個習慣——追完就把最後一集截圖存起來。不是要發文，只是為了下次有人問你的時候，能證明你真的在那裡待過。
反轉版：而那些你背得出片名、講得出上架日期的劇，通常都是你沒看的。躺在清單裡兩年，名字滾瓜爛熟，一集都沒點開。

en.content:
You just spent three nights finishing a forty-episode show.
You lost sleep over it, cried at it, and picked one genuine fight with a friend about it.

The next day a coworker asks, "What are you watching lately?"

You open your mouth and cannot remember the title.

So you start gesturing.
"It's the one where — okay, the guy's a lawyer."
"No, not that one. The one with the scene in the rain."
"Short hair, the woman, she moves to another city later on."
"The music is incredible, you've definitely heard the song."

Your coworker looks lost. You talk faster and get nowhere,
and finally give up: "Never mind, I'll text it to you."

Your memory is fine.
You remember which word his voice broke on, which side the camera was on when he cried,
you even remember where you were sitting that night.

You just never filed it as "a work."
It was never a title to you.
It was three nights when somebody kept you company.
en.editorNote: For the friend whose every recommendation starts with "that one with the actor from the other thing"; forgetting the name is not the opposite of it mattering
variations: Extended: eventually you start screenshotting the final episode when you finish. Not to post it, just so you can prove you were there next time somebody asks.
Reversal: meanwhile the titles you can recite perfectly, release date and all, are the ones you never watched. Two years on the list, name memorized, not a single episode opened.

items.sourceNote: 追劇 App 離線下載功能與觀眾實際使用落差（下載後未看、內容到期），原創改編

zh-tw.content:
出門前一晚，你花了四十分鐘做一件看起來很負責的事：
把八集下載到手機裡。

你甚至還挑了畫質。
你想像自己在飛機上，戴著耳機，優雅地看完三集，落地剛好追上進度。

實際發生的是：
起飛十分鐘你就睡著了。
中途醒來吃了餐、看了一眼窗外。
再睡。
落地。

那八集，一集都沒點開。

三個星期後，手機跳出一行提醒：
「您的離線內容即將到期。」

你盯著那行字，莫名覺得被說中了什麼。

下載從來不是為了看。
是為了在出發前那一刻相信——
接下來這幾天，你會有時間、會有心情、會是一個過得比較好的人。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個每次出門前都下載一整季、結果一集沒看的朋友；按下下載鍵那秒，我們買的是安心，不是內容
variations: 延伸版：同一件事你在很多地方做過：買了沒讀的書、報名沒去的課、存了兩百部的待看清單。你不是懶，你只是一直在替一個比較有空的自己打包行李。
反轉版：後來你學乖了，出門只下載一集。結果那一集你看完了，還意猶未盡地想再下一集——原來限制不是處罰，它把「終於看完一件事」還給了你。

en.content:
The night before the trip, you spent forty minutes on something that felt very responsible:
downloading eight episodes to your phone.

You even picked a video quality.
You pictured yourself on the plane, headphones on, calmly clearing three episodes, landing fully caught up.

What actually happened:
Asleep ten minutes after takeoff.
Woke up for the meal, looked out the window once.
Slept again.
Landed.

Zero of the eight episodes opened.

Three weeks later your phone says:
"Your downloaded content expires soon."

You stare at that sentence and feel oddly called out.

Downloading was never about watching.
It was about believing, in the moment before you left, that the next few days would come with time, and energy, and a slightly better version of you.
en.editorNote: For the friend who downloads a whole season before every trip and watches none of it; the download button sells reassurance, not content
variations: Extended: you've done this everywhere — the unread books, the class you signed up for, the two-hundred-title watchlist. You're not lazy. You keep packing luggage for a version of yourself with more free time.
Reversal: now you download exactly one episode before a trip. You finish it and immediately want another — turns out the limit wasn't a punishment. It handed back the feeling of finishing something.

items.sourceNote: 串流平台版權到期導致作品無預警下架、觀眾片單落空的普遍情形，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
你打開 App，想接著看第十九集。

搜尋列打了兩個字，跳出來的是「找不到相關內容」。

你以為自己打錯。重打一次。清快取。登出再登入。最後你把手機重開了——為了一部電視劇。

然後你在頁面最下面看到一行很小的字：因授權到期，本作品已於本月移除。

沒有通知、沒有倒數、沒有人問你追到第幾集。
它昨天還在。今天就不是這裡的東西了。

你連氣都不知道要氣誰。

你這才發現一件有點難堪的事：
那份「我收藏了好多劇」的安全感，
從頭到尾都是租來的。

你以為你在收藏。
你只是一直在借。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個把片單當資產在經營的朋友；串流時代我們沒有真的擁有任何一部劇，只是暫時被允許看
variations: 延伸版：那天晚上你做了一件很久沒做的事——把還沒看完的幾集全部離線存下來。你當然知道離線也會過期。你只是想替自己爭取一點時間。
反轉版：三年後它在另一個平台重新上線。你興沖沖點開，看了十分鐘就關掉。劇跟人一樣，隔太久再回來，回來的已經不是同一個你。

en.content:
You open the app to start episode nineteen.

You type two words into the search bar and get: "No matching titles."

You assume you spelled it wrong. Type it again. Clear the cache. Log out, log back in. You end up restarting your phone — over a television show.

Then you notice the fine print at the bottom of the page: this title was removed this month, licensing expired.

No notice. No countdown. Nobody asked how far in you were.
It was here yesterday. Today it isn't something that lives here.

You can't even work out who to be angry at.

And that's when the slightly embarrassing part lands:
that comfortable feeling of having a big collection
was rented the whole time.

You thought you were collecting.
You were only ever borrowing.
en.editorNote: For the friend who treats their watchlist like an asset portfolio; in the streaming era nobody owns a show, we're just permitted to watch it for now
variations: Extended: that night you do something you haven't done in ages — save every unwatched episode for offline. You know offline expires too. You're just buying yourself a little time.

Reversal: three years later it turns up on another service. You open it thrilled and close it ten minutes in. Shows are like people — come back after long enough and the one who came back isn't the same you.

items.sourceNote: 觀眾追劇時手機不離手、被畫面觸發衝動下單外送的行為觀察，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
劇裡演到晚上十一點半，男主角回家煮了一碗麵。

鏡頭只給了四秒。熱氣、蛋黃、一撮蔥花。

四秒之前，你躺得好好的。
四秒之後，你坐起來了。

你先去廚房站了一下，假裝在找東西。冰箱打開又關上，關上又打開，好像第二次會長出不一樣的內容。

最後你點開外送，湊到免運門檻，順手加了一份炸物，備註打上「不要辣」。

從按下暫停到下單完成，六分鐘。你這輩子沒有任何一件正事執行得這麼俐落。

麵送到的時候，你才想起來——
你根本不餓。

你只是想跟劇裡那個人吃同一頓飯，
確認熱的東西在你這邊也存在。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個看劇看到一半就默默打開外送的朋友；那個時間點下的單，通常跟餓沒什麼關係
variations: 延伸版：更荒謬的是東西送到你就把劇按停了，因為你想「專心吃」。你為了一部劇叫外送，又為了外送冷落那部劇。
反轉版：你發現這件事有時差——你想要的是畫面裡那碗麵，送到的永遠是別人家的味道。吃完你把進度往回拉，又看了一次那四秒。

en.content:
It's 11:30 PM in the show. The lead gets home and makes himself a bowl of noodles.

The shot lasts four seconds. Steam, egg yolk, a pinch of scallions.

Four seconds earlier you were lying down, perfectly fine.
Four seconds later you are sitting up.

First you go stand in the kitchen, pretending to look for something. Open the fridge, close it, open it again, as if round two might produce different contents.

Then you open the delivery app, add enough to clear the free-shipping minimum, throw in a side of something fried, and type "no spice" in the notes.

From pause button to order placed: six minutes. Nothing responsible in your life has ever moved that efficiently.

When the food arrives, it hits you —
you weren't hungry.

You just wanted to eat the same meal as the person on screen,
to confirm that hot food exists on this side of it too.
en.editorNote: For the friend who quietly opens a delivery app mid-episode; an order placed at that hour is rarely about hunger
variations: Extended: the truly absurd part is that when it arrives you pause the show, because you want to "focus on eating." You ordered because of a show, then neglected the show because of the order.
Reversal: there's a lag built into this — what you wanted was the bowl on screen, and what shows up is always somebody else's cooking. You finish it, scrub back, and watch those four seconds again.

items.sourceNote: 追劇行為量化研究與觀眾自行記錄、評分觀影紀錄的習慣，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
你裝了一個記錄追劇的 App。

一開始只是想記得自己看過什麼。
後來你開始給星星。
再後來，你會為了「這個月的圖表好看一點」，硬把一部很普通的劇看完。

月底它推給你一張報告：你今年看了 1,842 集，換算下來是 47 天。

你盯著那個數字，第一個反應不是驚訝，是心虛。

然後你偷偷想了一秒：那些看到一半就放掉的，如果也算進去，數字會不會更漂亮。

追劇本來是你生活裡唯一不用交成果的地方。
是你唯一可以爛尾、可以半途落跑、可以什麼都不留下的地方。

然後你親手，替它裝上了考核表。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個連休息都要統計和打分的朋友；有些事一開始計分，就不再是休息了
variations: 延伸版：你翻了一下自己給五顆星的清單，發現有一半你根本想不起演什麼。反而是那部你只給三顆星、卻在深夜看到眼眶熱的劇，有一句台詞你到現在還背得出來。分數從來沒有誠實過。
反轉版：那天你把 App 刪了。隔週朋友問你最近看什麼，你想了三秒說「一部還不錯的」，然後聊了四十分鐘。原來不記錄，你也記得。

en.content:
You installed an app to log what you watch.

At first it was just so you'd remember the titles.
Then you started giving out stars.
Then you started finishing mediocre shows so the month's chart would look better.

At the end of the month it hands you a report: 1,842 episodes this year. That's 47 days.

You stare at the number, and your first reaction isn't surprise. It's guilt.

Then, for one second, you catch yourself wondering whether the ones you abandoned halfway should count too, just to round it up.

Watching was the one part of your life that never asked for output.
The one place you were allowed to quit, drift off, and leave nothing behind.

And you went and bolted a performance review onto it.
en.editorNote: For the friend who tracks and rates even their downtime; the moment something gets scored, it stops being rest
variations: Extended: you scroll your five-star list and can't remember what half of it was about. Meanwhile the three-star one that wrecked you at 2 AM has a line you can still recite. The ratings were never the honest part.

Reversal: you deleted the app. A week later a friend asks what you've been watching, you think for three seconds, say "something decent, actually," and then talk about it for forty minutes. Turns out you remembered without the log.

items.sourceNote: 長壽演員跨世代作品、觀眾在新劇中認出多年前熟面孔的觀劇經驗，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
新劇第三集，一個配角走進畫面，你整個人停住。

「這個人我看過。」

你想不起是哪一部。你只記得他當年演的是那種會在雨裡跑、講話很大聲、非常年輕的角色。

現在他演一個父親。台詞不多，坐在餐桌邊，臉上多了幾道紋路，說話慢了半拍。

你把手機拿起來查，果然是他。

然後你順手算了一下：中間過了十四年。

你沒有為他難過。你是突然意識到——
那十四年，你也在。
你那時候在準備一場考試、在一間很小的租屋處、在一段後來沒有結果的關係裡。

原來追劇追久了會有這種副作用：
你以為你在看別人的人生，
其實你一直在拿他們的臉，替自己標記時間。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個在新劇裡認出老面孔、然後突然安靜下來的朋友；我們追的從來不只是劇，還有自己走過的那幾年
variations: 延伸版：從那天起你多了個習慣：看到熟悉的臉，你不查角色，你查他上一部戲是哪一年。你在用別人的作品年表，對照自己的。
反轉版：更奇怪的是有些人完全沒變。你看著他還是那張臉，才發現這幾年真正走樣的，只有你一個。

en.content:
Episode three of the new show. A supporting character walks into frame and you freeze.

"I know this person."

You can't place the title. All you remember is that he used to play the kind of role that runs through rain, talks too loud, and is extremely young.

Now he plays a father. Few lines. Sits at the dinner table. There are creases on his face and his speech runs half a beat slower.

You pick up your phone to check. It's him.

Then you do the math without meaning to: fourteen years.

You're not sad for him. What hits you is —
you were there for those fourteen years too.
Studying for something. Renting somewhere very small. Inside a relationship that didn't go anywhere.

So this is the side effect of watching for long enough:
you think you've been following other people's lives,
but you've been using their faces to mark the time in your own.
en.editorNote: For the friend who spots an old familiar face in a new show and goes quiet; we never just watch the show, we watch the years we spent getting here
variations: Extended: from then on you have a habit — when a face looks familiar, you don't look up the character, you look up what year his last project came out. You're using someone else's filmography as a ruler for your own.
Reversal: the strange ones are the actors who haven't changed at all. You look at the exact same face and realize the only thing visibly different, these past few years, is you.

items.sourceNote: 觀眾長期記憶會重構劇中台詞、重看時發現與記憶不符的普遍經驗，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
有一句台詞你記了很多年。

你把它抄在便條紙上貼過螢幕邊，低潮的時候拿出來唸，還在朋友難過的那天原封不動傳給他。

上個月你重看那部劇。

第七集，那個場景來了。燈光一樣，雨聲一樣，他轉過身，開口——

講的不是那句話。

你倒回去三次。你甚至把字幕語言換來換去，懷疑是翻譯的問題。

沒有。那句話不在裡面。

它是你在某個很難熬的晚上，把他講的半句、你自己想的半句，接起來的。

你當場有點慌，接著又鬆了一口氣。

原來這幾年撐著你的那句話，
本來就是你自己寫的。
你只是需要有人先開口，
你才敢承認那是你想說的。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個把某句台詞當護身符的朋友；記錯不是記憶出錯，是你偷偷替自己把那句話補完了
variations: 延伸版：後來你去搜那句話，發現網路上很多人也「記得」它，連標點都跟你記的一樣。大家在同一個地方記錯，因為大家在同一個地方需要它。
反轉版：更難解釋的是相反的情況——重看時你被某句話重重打中，查了一下才發現當年你確實看過。同一句話、同一個位置，只是那時候的你，還沒有需要它的理由。

en.content:
There's one line you've carried for years.

You wrote it on a sticky note and stuck it to the edge of your monitor. You said it to yourself on bad days. You once texted it, word for word, to a friend who was falling apart.

Last month you rewatched the show.

Episode seven. The scene arrives. Same lighting, same rain, he turns around, opens his mouth —

and says something else.

You rewind three times. You even switch subtitle languages, convinced it's a translation problem.

It isn't. The line isn't in there.

You built it on some unbearable night out of half of what he said and half of what you needed to hear.

You panic for a second, and then something loosens.

The sentence that held you up all these years
was yours the whole time.
You just needed somebody to speak first
before you'd admit you were the one saying it.
en.editorNote: For the friend who treats one line of dialogue like a lucky charm; misremembering isn't a memory failure, it's you quietly finishing the sentence for yourself
variations: Extended: you look the line up and find that plenty of strangers "remember" it too, punctuation and all. Everyone misremembers it in the same spot because everyone needs it in the same spot.

Reversal: the harder one is the opposite — a line knocks the wind out of you on a rewatch, and then you realize you'd already heard it years ago. Same words, same scene. You just didn't have a reason for it yet.

items.sourceNote: 2026 電信資費綁定串流會員的整合方案、觀眾為單一作品長期綁約的現象，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
你原本只是想看一部劇。

朋友說那部在某個平台獨家，你查了月費，覺得有點貴。

然後你在電信官網看到一個方案：升級資費，附贈兩年串流會員，每個月只多一點點。

你在腦中算了三分鐘的數學，得出一個非常有說服力的結論：這樣比較划算。

你簽了二十四個月。

那部劇，你花九天看完。

現在是第七個月。你偶爾打開那個 App，滑一滑，關掉。首頁推薦的東西你一部都不想看，但你會跟自己說：反正錢已經付了。

帳單每個月準時提醒你——
你曾經多想看一部劇。

劇已經完結了。
合約還沒有。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個為了一部劇升級資費、結果被綁到明年的朋友；我們很常用兩年的承諾，去換一個星期的興奮
variations: 延伸版：更好笑的是剩下的十七個月你真的會偶爾用到它。不是因為想看，是因為每次想放棄的時候，你都會想起自己還在付錢。原來沉沒成本也可以是一種陪伴。
反轉版：合約到期那天你打去解約，客服問原因，你說「沒在看了」。掛掉電話卻有點悵然——當初讓你眼睛一亮、二話不說就簽下去的那股衝動，才是你真正想留住的東西。

en.content:
You just wanted to watch one show.

A friend said it was exclusive to some platform. You checked the monthly price and winced.

Then your phone carrier's site offered you a deal: upgrade your plan, get two years of that streaming service bundled in, for only a little more per month.

You did three minutes of mental math and arrived at a deeply persuasive conclusion: this is the cheaper option.

You signed for twenty-four months.

The show took you nine days.

It's now month seven. Occasionally you open the app, scroll, close it. Nothing on the homepage appeals to you, but you tell yourself it's already paid for.

The bill arrives on time every month to remind you
how badly you once wanted to watch one show.

The show has ended.
The contract has not.
en.editorNote: For the friend who upgraded a phone plan over one series and is locked in until next year; we routinely trade a two-year commitment for one week of excitement
variations: Extended: the funny part is you do use it occasionally for the remaining seventeen months. Not because you want to — because every time you think about quitting, you remember you're still paying. Turns out sunk cost can double as company.

Reversal: on the day it expires you call to cancel and the rep asks why. "Not watching anymore," you say. You hang up feeling oddly hollow — the thing you actually wanted to keep was that flash of wanting something enough to sign without thinking.

items.sourceNote: 追劇後立即查看網路評價、以他人評論校正自身感受的觀眾行為，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
最後一集播完，畫面暗下去。

你坐在原地沒動，心臟還在跳，眼眶是熱的。

然後你做了一件很奇怪的事：
你沒有讓自己安靜三分鐘，
你打開了討論區。

你想看看別人怎麼說。

第一則說結局收得太草。第二則說前面很好、後段崩了。第三則列出七個邏輯漏洞，還附上時間軸。

你一則一則往下滑，滑到某個瞬間，發現剛才那份感動正在慢慢縮小。

十分鐘後你關掉手機，心裡的說法已經改成：「其實還好啦，中上。」

可是你剛剛明明哭了。

沒有人規定你要跟誰一致。
你的眼淚不需要通過任何人的審核，
它掉下來的那一秒，就已經是真的了。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個看完劇一定先滑完評價才敢下結論的朋友；感受不是投票，不用等別人開票
variations: 延伸版：反過來也發生過——你本來覺得普通，但整個網路都在瘋，於是你默默把它放進「我很愛的劇」那一欄。你不是在追劇，你是在對答案。
反轉版：後來你只改了一件事：看完先什麼都不做，坐十分鐘，把當下的感覺打進自己的備忘錄，然後才去看別人怎麼講。你發現兩件事可以並存，只要你先說話。

en.content:
The finale ends. The screen goes dark.

You don't move. Your heart is still going and your eyes are hot.

Then you do something strange:
instead of sitting with it for three minutes,
you open the discussion thread.

You want to see what other people said.

First comment: the ending was rushed. Second: strong setup, total collapse in the back half. Third: seven plot holes, with timestamps.

You scroll, and somewhere in there you feel the thing you were feeling start to shrink.

Ten minutes later you put the phone down, and the version in your head has become: "It was fine, I guess. Above average."

But you were crying a minute ago.

Nobody requires your reaction to match anyone else's.
Your tears don't need to clear review.
They were true the second they showed up.
en.editorNote: For the friend who can't decide how they feel until they've read the comments; feeling something isn't a vote, you don't have to wait for the count
variations: Extended: it runs the other way too — you thought it was okay, the whole internet lost its mind, and you quietly filed it under "shows I love." That's not watching. That's checking your answers against the key.

Reversal: eventually you changed one thing: after the finale, do nothing for ten minutes, type what you actually felt into your own notes, and only then go read the thread. Both can exist. You just have to speak first.

items.sourceNote: 家庭共用串流帳號、從「繼續觀看」列讀出家人近況的日常觀察，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
家裡的串流帳號是共用的。

你點進去想接昨天的進度，第一排「繼續觀看」卻不太像你的。

一部家庭劇停在第三十四集。一個很吵的綜藝停在中間。還有一部你完全沒印象的紀錄片，關於某一種鳥。

你知道那是誰的。

你媽從來不跟你聊她在看什麼。她只會問你吃飽沒、什麼時候回家。

但那排片單會說話。

它說她最近喜歡溫和的東西。說她某一天看到一半就睡著了。也說上個月有整整一週，她什麼都沒點開——那一週你剛好沒打電話回家。

你什麼都沒問。

你只是往下滑，找到自己那一部，按下播放，
心裡想著：下次回去，可以問她那部關於鳥的紀錄片好不好看。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個跟家人共用一個追劇帳號的朋友；那排「繼續觀看」是很多家庭裡，唯一還在互相更新的近況
variations: 延伸版：後來你多做了一件事——把你覺得她會喜歡的劇偷偷加進共用清單，不說是誰加的。過幾天你看見那部的進度條動了。你們就用這種方式聊天，一句話都不用講。
反轉版：也有另一種版本：某天那排片單完全停住了，很久沒有新的進度。你才意識到，原來你一直在用它確認家裡的人今天過得還可以。

en.content:
The streaming account at home is shared.

You open it to pick up where you left off, and the top row — Continue Watching — doesn't quite look like yours.

A family drama paused on episode thirty-four. A loud variety show stopped mid-episode. A documentary you've never heard of, about a particular kind of bird.

You know whose those are.

Your mom never tells you what she's watching. She asks whether you've eaten and when you're coming home.

But that row talks.

It says she's been wanting gentle things lately. It says she fell asleep partway through on some night. It says there was a full week last month when she opened nothing at all — the same week you didn't call.

You don't ask about any of it.

You scroll past, find your own show, hit play,
and think: next time I'm home, I'll ask her if the bird one is any good.
en.editorNote: For the friend sharing one account with family; in a lot of households that Continue Watching row is the only status update anybody still posts
variations: Extended: eventually you start adding shows you think she'd like to the shared list without saying they're from you. A few days later the progress bar on one of them has moved. That's the conversation. Neither of you says a word.

Reversal: there's another version of this: one day the row stops changing, and stays stopped for a long while. That's when you realize you'd been using it to confirm that everyone at home was doing okay.

items.sourceNote: 串流平台整併、內容庫搬家導致觀看進度重置的使用者經驗，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
你追到第二十二集的那部劇，換家了。

平台整併，App 要重灌，帳號要重新登入，公告寫得很客氣：「內容將完整移轉，敬請安心觀賞。」

內容確實移轉了。
你的進度沒有。

新首頁乾乾淨淨，「繼續觀看」那一排是空的，像沒有人在這裡住過。

你有點惱。惱的不是要重找，是那條進度條被清掉的感覺——
好像那二十二個晚上，系統這邊沒有紀錄。

然後你點進劇集列表，手指往下滑。

第二十二集的縮圖跳出來的瞬間，你就認出來了。
雨天、醫院走廊、他手裡那把沒撐開的傘。

你連他站在那裡幾秒都記得。

原來需要備份的從來不是進度條。
你看過的東西是存在你身上的，
換哪一個 App 都不會不見。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個平台一整併就要重找進度的朋友；紀錄可以被清空，看過的感覺不會
variations: 延伸版：後來你養成一個習慣——每追完一集，在備忘錄打一行「第幾集，發生什麼」。不是怕忘，是想留下自己當時看的樣子。那份紀錄沒有任何平台收得回去。
反轉版：也有另一種結果：進度沒了，你乾脆從第一集重看。看到第七集才發現，這次你注意到的完全是另一批細節。清空有時候不是損失，是又給了你一次第一遍。

en.content:
The show you were twenty-two episodes into has moved house.

The platforms merged. New app, new login, and a very polite notice: "All content will transfer in full. Enjoy with confidence."

The content did transfer.
Your progress didn't.

The new home screen is spotless. The Continue Watching row is empty, like nobody ever lived here.

It annoys you. Not the hunting for your place — the feeling of a progress bar being wiped.
As if, on their side, those twenty-two nights were never logged.

So you open the episode list and scroll.

The second the thumbnail for episode twenty-two loads, you know it.
Rain, hospital corridor, the umbrella in his hand he never opened.

You even remember how long he stood there.

Turns out the progress bar was never the thing that needed backing up.
What you've watched is stored in you.
No app switch is going to take it.
en.editorNote: For the friend who has to re-find their place every time a service gets absorbed by another one; the record can be wiped, the watching can't
variations: Extended: eventually you start typing one line per episode into your notes — number, what happened. Not because you'd forget, but because you want to keep what it looked like from where you were sitting. No platform can claw that back.

Reversal: there's another outcome: progress gone, so you just start over from episode one. By episode seven you notice you're catching a completely different set of details. Sometimes a wipe isn't a loss, it's a second first time.

items.sourceNote: 深夜戴耳機追劇、情緒高漲卻必須壓抑出聲的觀眾日常，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
半夜一點，全家都睡了。

你把音量調到剛好，戴上耳機，跟自己說只看一集。

然後那場戲來了。

男主角站在門口，話講到一半停住，轉身就走。

你整個人炸開——
想罵人、想拍大腿、想大喊「你回來把話講完」。

但你不能出聲。

於是你在黑暗裡完成了一整套無聲表演：
嘴巴張到最大，一點聲音都沒有。
拳頭捶在棉被上，怕發出聲響，力道還特地收一半。
眼淚掉下來，你連吸鼻子都是分三次慢慢吸的。

隔天早上家人問：「昨天睡得好嗎？」
你說：「還可以。」

沒有人知道你凌晨兩點在那個房間裡經歷了什麼。

有些情緒本來就不需要觀眾。
只要有人真的感覺過，它就成立了——
那個人是你自己，也算數。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個半夜戴耳機追劇、情緒炸開卻不能出聲的朋友；沒人看見的感動也是真的感動
variations: 延伸版：你甚至發展出一套無聲詞彙——手掌拍空氣＝這也太甜；捂臉往後倒＝我不行了；坐直、暫停、深呼吸＝這段我要再看一次。全套動作只有你自己看得懂。
反轉版：直到某天你一回頭，看見門縫那裡站著人。你媽問：「你剛剛是在哭還是在笑？」你想了三秒，誠實回答：「兩個都有。」

en.content:
One in the morning. Everyone else is asleep.

You set the volume just right, put your headphones on, and tell yourself: one episode.

Then the scene happens.

He stops mid-sentence in the doorway, turns around, and leaves.

Something detonates in you —
you want to yell, slap the mattress, shout "get back here and finish that sentence."

But you can't make a sound.

So you deliver an entire silent performance in the dark:
mouth open as wide as it goes, nothing coming out.
Fist into the duvet, at half power, in case it thumps.
Tears come, and you split each sniff into three quiet ones.

Next morning someone asks, "Sleep okay?"
You say, "Yeah, fine."

Nobody knows what happened in that room at two a.m.

Some feelings were never going to need an audience.
They count as long as somebody actually felt them —
and you're somebody.
en.editorNote: For the friend who watches in headphones at 1 a.m. and has to detonate in total silence; a reaction nobody saw is still a real reaction
variations: Extended: you've even built a silent vocabulary — palm slapping the air = that was too sweet; hands over face, falling backward = I cannot; sitting up, pausing, deep breath = I'm rewatching that. Fluent in a language with exactly one speaker.

Reversal: until the night you turn around and there's someone in the gap of the door. Your mom asks, "Were you crying or laughing just now?" You think about it for three seconds and answer honestly: "Both."

items.sourceNote: 劇迷推薦時記得畫面卻想不起劇名、只能用關鍵字反查的行為，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
朋友問你有沒有劇可以推薦。

你說有，超好看，我上個月才追完。

然後你卡住了。

你想不起來它叫什麼。

你記得男主角在雨裡等了一整夜。記得女主角把那封信摺了三次才放進口袋。記得倒數第二集有一個長達八秒、一句台詞都沒有的對望。

你就是想不起來劇名。

你打開搜尋列，輸入你唯一的線索：

「電視劇 男主 失憶 下雨 信摺三次」

第一則跳出一部你沒聽過的泰劇，第二則是減肥廣告。

你笑出來，改打：「那部很好看的 男女主角最後在車站」。

你查了十二分鐘才把它找回來。

但你有沒有發現——
你忘掉的是名字，
你記得的全是它讓你有感覺的那幾秒。

那才是它真正的名字。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個推劇永遠想不起劇名、只能拚命形容畫面的朋友；記不住名字不代表你沒認真看
variations: 延伸版：後來你在備忘錄開了一頁，只寫關鍵畫面：「雨、傘、沒講完的那句」。這比記劇名好用——過半年再看，名字喚不起什麼，那三個詞一秒就把你拉回去。
反轉版：更慘的版本是：你查了半天終於找到，興沖沖傳給朋友。他回：「這部就是我上個月推薦給你的啊。」

en.content:
A friend asks if you have anything to recommend.

You say yes, it's so good, I finished it last month.

Then you stall.

You cannot remember what it's called.

You remember him waiting in the rain all night. You remember her folding that letter three times before it went in her pocket. You remember an eight-second look with no dialogue in the second-to-last episode.

You just can't remember the title.

So you open the search bar and type in the only evidence you have:

"tv show male lead amnesia rain letter folded three times"

First result is a Thai drama you've never heard of. Second is a weight loss ad.

You laugh and try again: "that really good show they end up at the train station."

It takes you twelve minutes to find it.

But notice what happened —
what you forgot was the name.
What you kept was every second of it that made you feel something.

That's the actual title.
en.editorNote: For the friend who can never produce a title and has to describe the scene instead; forgetting the name doesn't mean you weren't paying attention
variations: Extended: eventually you keep a page in your notes with nothing but images — "rain, umbrella, the sentence he never finished." It beats titles. Six months out, a name jogs nothing and those three words drop you right back in.
Reversal: the worse version: you finally track it down, send it to your friend all excited, and he replies, "That's the one I recommended to you last month."

items.sourceNote: 觀眾能連刷八集卻遲遲按不下新劇第一集的啟動門檻現象，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
你的追劇能力其實是分裂的。

一旦開始，你可以一個晚上連看八集，中間只起身兩次，一次拿水一次上廁所。

但那部躺在清單裡三個月的劇，你就是按不下去。

不是不好看。朋友說好看，評價說好看，你自己看預告的時候也心動。

你只是每次滑到它，都想著「今天有點累，改天」。

後來你想通一件事：

看第九集不需要力氣，因為那些人你都認識了。
看第一集需要力氣，因為你得從頭認識一群陌生人，記他們的名字、關係、誰跟誰有過節。

而今天的你，連回訊息都嫌費力，實在沒有多的力氣再去認識任何人。

所以那不是懶。

那是你今天的電量，剛好只夠陪已經熟的人。

改天再開始也沒關係，
那些人不會走，他們會待在第一集裡等你。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個能連刷八集、卻對新劇第一集卡三個月的朋友；開始比繼續更耗力氣，這很正常
variations: 延伸版：所以你的清單自動分成兩區——一區是「新的、要重新認識人的」，一區是「舊的、閉著眼睛都能進去的」。累的那幾週，你永遠只在第二區活動。這不叫沒進度，這叫知道自己現在需要什麼。
反轉版：而真正開始的那天通常也沒什麼理由。你只是某個晚上心情剛好鬆了一點，順手按下播放，然後凌晨三點看到第六集，回頭想：我到底在猶豫三個月什麼。

en.content:
Your binge-watching ability is, technically, two different abilities.

Once you start, you can do eight episodes in a night, standing up exactly twice: water, bathroom.

But that show that's been sitting in your list for three months? You cannot press play on it.

It's not that it looks bad. Friends say it's good, reviews say it's good, the trailer got you.

It's just that every time you scroll past it you think: kind of tired today, another time.

Then it clicks:

Episode nine costs nothing, because you already know those people.
Episode one costs something, because you have to meet a whole room of strangers — names, who's related to who, who wronged who.

And today you can barely answer a text. You do not have the energy to meet anyone new.

So it isn't laziness.

It's that today's battery covers exactly the people you already know.

Starting another day is fine.
They're not going anywhere. They'll be in episode one, waiting.
en.editorNote: For the friend who can clear eight episodes in a night but has been stuck on episode one of something new for three months; starting costs more than continuing, and that's normal
variations: Extended: so your list quietly splits in two — the new ones, where you'd have to meet people, and the old ones you could walk into with your eyes closed. On the tired weeks you only ever live in the second half. That's not a lack of progress, that's knowing what you need right now.

Reversal: and the night you finally start usually has no reason behind it. Something in you loosens a little, your thumb hits play, and at three a.m. you're on episode six thinking: what exactly was I hesitating about for three months?

items.sourceNote: 季與季之間動輒兩年空窗、平台以前情提要接回觀眾的現象，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
你等的那部劇，第二季隔了兩年才回來。

上線那天你點開，平台很貼心，先播三分鐘前情提要。

畫面閃過那些你當年哭到不行的橋段——那句台詞、那個轉身、那個沒說出口的名字。

你看著，覺得有點陌生。

不是忘記，是感覺對不上了。

兩年前你為它熬夜到三點，隔天頂著黑眼圈上班，還是覺得值得。
兩年後你看到一半，先起身把洗衣機裡的衣服拿去晾。

劇裡的人一天都沒老，還站在你離開時的那個路口。

只有你，換過一份工作、搬過一次家、認真喜歡過一個人又結束了。

所以那不是劇變難看了。

是它停在原地等你，而你已經走到別的地方。

你還是把第二季追完了。

不是為了劇情，
是為了跟兩年前那個為它掉眼淚的自己，好好道別。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個等第二季等了兩年、回來卻發現心情對不上的朋友；不是劇變了，是你走遠了
variations: 延伸版：所以「等太久」的代價從來不是忘記劇情。前情提要可以幫你補上誰死了、誰走了，補不回你當年守在螢幕前的那個晚上。
反轉版：但也有另一種情況——你以為自己早就不在乎了，結果主題曲前奏才響三秒，眼眶就熱了。原來有些東西不是被時間帶走，只是被你收好而已。

en.content:
That show you were waiting on finally came back. Season two, two years later.

You hit play on release day, and the platform is thoughtful about it: three minutes of "previously on."

All the moments that wrecked you back then flash by — the line, the turn, the name nobody said out loud.

And you watch it feeling faintly like a stranger.

Not because you forgot. Because it doesn't land the same.

Two years ago you stayed up until three for this and went to work wrecked and thought it was worth it.
Two years later you pause halfway through to move the laundry.

Nobody on screen has aged a day. They're still standing exactly where you left them.

You're the one who changed jobs, moved apartments, loved someone properly and watched it end.

So it's not that the show got worse.

It waited for you in the same spot, and you walked somewhere else.

You finished season two anyway.

Not for the plot.
To say a decent goodbye to the person who cried over it two years ago.
en.editorNote: For the friend who waited two years for season two and came back feeling out of sync with it; the show didn't change, you did
variations: Extended: so the real cost of a long wait was never forgetting the plot. The recap can tell you who died and who left. It can't give you back the night you sat there caring that much.

Reversal: though sometimes it goes the other way — you're sure you've moved on, then three seconds of the theme song play and your eyes sting. Turns out time didn't take it. You just put it away somewhere.

items.sourceNote: 串流時代季集數大幅縮短、劇情密度變高的趨勢，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
以前一季二十二集。

中間總有幾集根本沒什麼事發生——一群人擠在廚房搶一鍋東西吃、有人搬家、有人為了一件不重要的小事吵一場。

那些集數，當年你邊看邊想：這集到底在幹嘛。

現在一季六集。

每一集都在推進度，每一集都有訊息量，第三集就要你哭，第六集直接收尾。整季看完只花一個下午。

很有效率。

但你發現一件事：你記不住他們。

因為你會喜歡一個角色，從來不是因為他的高光時刻。

是因為那些沒事發生的集數——他怎麼吃飯、無聊的時候在幹嘛、被冷落的時候臉會垮到什麼程度。

那些「浪費掉」的時間，才是你認識一個人的方式。

這點跟現實一模一樣。

你最熟的那幾個人，也不是在什麼大事裡認識的，
是在很多什麼都沒發生的日子裡，慢慢變熟的。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個抱怨「現在一季只有六集，看完沒感情」的朋友；感情是靠沒事發生的時間養出來的
variations: 延伸版：所以你會特別懷念某些老劇裡最沒劇情的那一集。很多年後你記得的不是誰報了仇，是他們四個人在廚房搶一鍋麵。
反轉版：當然六集也有六集的好，至少你不會被四十集的誤會折磨。只是看完的隔天，你連一個角色的口頭禪都想不起來。

en.content:
Seasons used to be twenty-two episodes.

A few of them were about nothing. Four people fighting over one pot of food in a kitchen. Somebody moving apartments. An argument about something that didn't matter.

Back then you watched those and thought: what is this episode even for.

Now a season is six episodes.

Every one advances the plot. Every one carries information. Episode three makes you cry, episode six wraps it up. You can finish the whole thing in an afternoon.

Very efficient.

And then you notice something: you can't remember them.

Because you never loved a character for their big moment.

You loved them for the nothing episodes — how they eat, what they do when they're bored, exactly how their face falls when they get left out.

That "wasted" time was the whole way you got to know someone.

Which is how it works off screen too.

The people you know best, you didn't meet in a crisis.
You got there across a lot of days where nothing happened at all.
en.editorNote: For the friend complaining that six-episode seasons leave them feeling nothing; attachment is built out of the filler
variations: Extended: which is why the episode you miss most from an old show is usually the one with no plot in it. Years later you don't remember who got revenge. You remember four people fighting over one pot of noodles.
Reversal: six episodes has its upsides, obviously — nobody drags one misunderstanding across forty of them. It's just that the next morning you can't name a single character's catchphrase.

items.sourceNote: 觀眾刻意保留最後一集不看以延後結束感的追劇行為，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
那部劇你追到只剩最後一集，然後你停在那裡，停了兩個禮拜。

朋友問：「你看完沒？」
你說：「快了，最近有點忙。」

你沒有忙。你昨天晚上還看完了兩集你根本不在乎的節目。

真相是——

只要你不點下去，這個故事就還沒結束。

他們就還在那個城市裡過日子，還沒有人要離開，還沒有人講出那句你已經預感到、聽了會難過的話。

最後一集躺在那裡，像一封你不敢拆的信。

你很清楚拆開之後會怎樣：
看完、畫面暗掉、片尾跑完，然後房間安靜下來，安靜到你聽得見自己在懷念一件五分鐘前才結束的事。

所以你先不看。

這不是拖延。

這是你能為一個很喜歡的東西做的、最後一件溫柔的事——

讓它多活兩個禮拜。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個追到剩最後一集就故意卡住的人；不是沒時間，是捨不得親手把它結束
variations: 延伸版：而你真的按下播放的那天，通常是某個心情剛好很穩的晚上。你會先泡杯熱的、把群組通知關掉、坐正一點——像在準備送一個要出遠門的朋友。
反轉版：也有另一種人，最後一集當天就看完，然後空虛三天。兩種都不算錯，一種是先痛完再說，一種是分期付款。

en.content:
You got to the last episode and then you just... stopped. For two weeks.

A friend asks if you finished it.
You say almost, work's been busy.

Work has not been busy. Last night you watched two episodes of something you don't care about at all.

The truth is:

As long as you don't press play, the story isn't over.

They're all still living in that city. Nobody has left yet. Nobody has said the line you can already feel coming, the one that's going to hurt.

The finale sits there like a letter you're not ready to open.

You know exactly how it goes: you watch it, the screen goes dark, the credits run out, and the room gets quiet — quiet enough that you can hear yourself already missing something that ended five minutes ago.

So not yet.

This isn't procrastination.

It's the last kind thing you can do for something you loved:

let it live two more weeks.
en.editorNote: For the person parked on the final episode on purpose; it's not a scheduling problem, they just don't want to be the one who ends it
variations: Extended: and the night you finally play it is usually a night you feel steady. You make something hot, mute the group chat, sit up a little straighter — like seeing a friend off at the airport.
Reversal: other people watch the finale the day it drops and float around hollow for three days. Neither is wrong. One pays for it all at once, the other in installments.

items.sourceNote: 以熟悉舊劇作為助眠背景、反覆卡在同一集開頭的觀看習慣，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
你有一部劇，是專門用來睡著的。

不是因為難看，是相反——它太熟了。

你看過三遍，知道每一個轉折，知道誰會被誤會、誰會回頭、最後誰跟誰在一起。

所以你可以放心地睡。

結果就是：第三集的前十分鐘，你看過九次。

每次都是那個開場、那首歌、那個人推開門講第一句話——然後就沒有記憶了。

隔天早上醒來，螢幕還亮著，進度條停在四十八分鐘。

你從來沒有正常地從第三集走到第四集過。

但你一點也不介意。

因為你要的本來就不是後續。

你要的是有人在旁邊講話，聲音穩定、語氣熟悉，而且接下來會發生什麼你全部都知道——

在一個什麼都不確定的日子結束之後，
這大概是你能給自己最便宜的安全感。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個每晚放同一部舊劇助眠、同一集開頭看過八次的人；那不是追劇，是有人陪著入睡
variations: 延伸版：所以真正的睡前神劇有三個條件——你看過、你愛過，而且它不會在半夜突然丟一個讓你完全清醒的轉折給你。
反轉版：唯一的風險是某天你不小心真的看下去了，凌晨三點在床上重看完第四到第八集，隔天頂著黑眼圈罵自己：這部明明是拿來睡覺的。

en.content:
You have one show that exists purely to fall asleep to.

Not because it's bad. The opposite — you know it too well.

You've seen it three times. You know every turn, who gets misread, who comes back, who ends up with who.

So you can let go and sleep.

Which means: you have watched the first ten minutes of episode three nine times.

Same cold open, same song, same person pushing a door open and saying the first line — and then nothing.

You wake up, the screen is still on, the progress bar is parked at forty-eight minutes.

You have never once made it from episode three to episode four like a normal person.

And you don't mind at all.

Because you were never in it for what happens next.

You wanted someone talking nearby — steady voice, familiar cadence, and absolutely no surprises about what's coming.

After a day where nothing was certain,
that's about the cheapest safety money can buy.
en.editorNote: For the person who falls asleep to the same old show every night and has seen that cold open eight times; that's not watching, that's company
variations: Extended: so the perfect sleep show has three requirements — you've seen it, you loved it, and it will not spring a twist on you at midnight that wakes you all the way up.

Reversal: the one risk is the night you accidentally keep watching, finish episodes four through eight at three a.m., and spend the next day annoyed at yourself: that one was supposed to be for sleeping.

items.sourceNote: 觀眾長年抱怨串流影集夜戲過暗、調亮度也無效的現象，原創改編

zh-tw.content:
那部劇的第九集，是一場夜戲。

你先把房間的燈關掉。
沒用。

你把窗簾拉上，把亮著的手機翻面蓋住，連冰箱的燈都覺得礙事。
還是看不到。

你把亮度推到最大，畫面沒有變亮，只是原本黑的地方，變成比較亮的黑。

你甚至拿袖子把螢幕擦了一遍，一邊擦一邊懷疑是自己太髒。

最後你是用聽的看完那場戲：
有人跌倒、有人喊了一聲、有東西掉在地上——
你完全不知道誰打了誰，但你知道結束了。

隔天你上網找討論，第一則熱門留言只有五個字：
「有人看得到嗎？」

下面兩千個人在回覆。

那一刻你反而安心了。

不是你的電視太爛，也不是你的眼睛老了，
是全世界都在對著一片黑，假裝自己看懂了。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個為了看清楚一場夜戲，關燈、拉窗簾、擦螢幕全都做過一遍的人；也適合貼在「這集到底在演什麼」的討論串裡
variations: 延伸版：追劇族的新技能是用聽的補完夜戲——腳步聲判斷有幾個人，喘氣聲判斷誰快撐不住，配樂一收就知道倒下的不是主角。
反轉版：更氣的是隔天白天重看一次，你才發現那場黑漆漆的戲根本不重要，真正的關鍵是下一集有人在早餐桌上，很亮很清楚地講的那一句話。

en.content:
Episode nine is a night scene.

First you turn off the lights in the room.
Nothing.

You close the curtains, flip your glowing phone face down, and start resenting the light inside the fridge.
Still nothing.

You push the brightness to maximum. The picture doesn't get brighter — the black parts just become a slightly brighter black.

At one point you wipe the screen with your sleeve, half convinced the problem is that you're dirty.

In the end you watch that scene with your ears:
somebody falls, somebody shouts, something hits the floor —
you have no idea who hit who, but you can tell it's over.

The next day you go looking for a discussion thread. The top comment is four words:
"Could anyone see that?"

Two thousand people are replying under it.

And somehow that's a relief.

Your TV isn't broken and your eyes aren't going.
The whole world is staring into the same darkness, pretending it followed along.
en.editorNote: For the person who killed the lights, drew the curtains, and cleaned the screen just to make out one night scene; also good in a "what actually happened in this episode" thread
variations: Extended: seasoned bingers now reconstruct night scenes by ear — footsteps tell you how many people, breathing tells you who's losing, and the second the score drops out you know it wasn't the lead who went down.

Reversal: the real insult is rewatching in daylight and realizing that pitch-black scene barely mattered — the thing that changes everything is one line somebody says at a breakfast table next episode, brightly lit and perfectly clear.

items.sourceNote: 串流平台介面設計（集數標題、預覽縮圖）如何影響觀看體驗的研究，原創改編為介面自爆雷情境

zh-tw.content:
你躲了兩個禮拜的雷，最後是平台自己爆給你的。

這兩個禮拜，你不看預告、不點討論區、朋友傳訊息來一律先問「有沒有雷」。
你連熱門排行都不敢滑，因為封面會動。

然後你打開 App，準備按第十三集。

集數列表上，第十四集的標題就大大方方地寫在那裡：
〈告別〉

旁邊配一張縮圖：一群人站在雨裡，而其中一個人不在畫面上。

你手還沒離開遙控器，就已經知道接下來三集要發生什麼事。

你防了兩個禮拜的社群、群組、限時動態，
沒有任何一個人爆到你。

真正把結局丟到你臉上的，
是那個每個月準時跟你收錢的地方。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個躲雷躲到極致、最後被平台自家集數標題爆掉的人；截圖丟追劇群組保證一片哀嚎
variations: 延伸版：所以老練的追劇族看集數列表時，眼睛是刻意散焦的——只認數字，不讀標題，不看縮圖，像在雷區裡走路。
反轉版：更氣的是你截圖去罵，朋友回你「這標題超普通啊」——雷只會炸給真的在看的人，這是最公平，也是最殘忍的地方。

en.content:
You dodged spoilers for two weeks, and then the platform spoiled it for you itself.

For two weeks: no trailers, no comment sections, every message from a friend answered with "wait, is that a spoiler?" first.
You stopped scrolling the trending row because the cover art moves.

Then you open the app to hit episode thirteen.

And there, in the episode list, sits the title of episode fourteen, in plain confident text:
"Goodbye."

Next to it, a thumbnail: a group of people standing in the rain, and one of them isn't in the frame.

Your hand hasn't even left the remote and you already know what the next three episodes are going to do to you.

Two weeks of guarding against group chats, feeds, and stories.
Not one person got you.

The thing that threw the ending in your face
was the service that charges your card on the first of every month.
en.editorNote: For the spoiler-dodging champion taken out by their own streaming app's episode list; screenshot it into the group chat and watch everyone groan
variations: Extended: which is why experienced bingers now read episode lists slightly out of focus — numbers only, no titles, no thumbnails, moving through it like a minefield.

Reversal: the worst part is screenshotting it to complain and having a friend reply "that title seems totally normal?" — spoilers only detonate for people who are actually watching, which is both the fairest and cruelest part.

items.sourceNote: 深夜追劇時數統計與行動裝置觀看情境，原創改編為藍牙耳機延遲／單邊沒電的深夜場景

zh-tw.content:
半夜追劇的人，跟一副藍牙耳機的關係很複雜。

先是延遲。
嘴巴動完半秒，聲音才追上來。你一開始沒察覺，直到有人講話講到一半停住，你才發現自己看的是一部對不準的劇。

重新連線一次，好了。

接著是左邊那隻。
它先走一步，在最安靜的那句台詞正中間「嗶」了一聲，然後世界只剩一半。

你不敢外放，因為隔壁房間有人在睡。

所以你維持了一個非常可笑的姿勢：
右耳戴著，左手把手機貼在左耳旁邊，音量調到二，整個人縮成一團。

就這樣看完了一集。

隔天有人問你昨晚睡得好嗎，你說還好。

你沒說的是：
你昨天為了不吵醒任何人，用單邊耳機和一半的音量，把一部劇追到了兩點半。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個為了不吵到家人，戴單邊耳機、把手機貼著耳朵看到半夜的人；深夜追劇群組的共鳴彈
variations: 延伸版：真正的深夜追劇裝備清單只有三樣——一副撐得住的耳機、一條伸手就拿得到的充電線，以及把音量停在「聽得到台詞、聽不到自己心虛」的那個刻度。
反轉版：最崩潰的是耳機兩隻都沒電，你只好把它們丟回盒子裡充電，跟自己說「那就先睡吧」——然後你打開了手機的擴音，音量一，臉貼上去，繼續看。

en.content:
People who binge at 1 a.m. have a complicated relationship with one pair of earbuds.

First, the lag.
Mouths finish moving half a second before the sound catches up. You don't notice at first — not until someone stops mid-sentence and you realize the whole show has been slightly out of sync.

Reconnect. Fixed.

Then the left one goes.
It quits early, with a bright little beep landing directly on the quietest line in the episode, and half your world disappears.

You can't use the speaker. Someone is asleep in the next room.

So you hold a genuinely ridiculous position:
right bud in, left hand pressing the phone against your left ear, volume on two, entire body curled into a ball.

And you finish the episode like that.

The next day someone asks if you slept well. You say fine.

What you leave out is that in order to not wake a single person in the house, you finished a show at 2:30 in the morning on one earbud and half the volume.
en.editorNote: For the person who watched until 2 a.m. on one earbud with a phone pressed to their ear so nobody else would wake up; a direct hit in any late-night watch thread
variations: Extended: the real late-night binge kit is three items — earbuds with enough battery to survive, a charging cable within arm's reach, and the volume parked at exactly the notch where you can hear the dialogue but not your own guilt.

Reversal: peak collapse is both buds dying, putting them back in the case, telling yourself "fine, bedtime" — and then turning on the phone speaker at volume one, face two inches from the screen, and continuing.

items.sourceNote: 在床上以行動裝置追劇的觀看習慣統計，原創改編為手機砸臉／落枕的身體代價

zh-tw.content:
躺著用手機追劇的人，都經歷過那一下。

手舉在臉的正上方，撐了二十分鐘，手臂開始發麻。
你改成側躺，畫面歪了，於是你把頭也歪過去，兩個一起歪。

然後你的眼皮鬆了半秒——

手機正面砸在鼻樑上。

你痛到整個人坐起來，第一個動作不是揉鼻子，
是看螢幕：剛剛那段漏掉多少。

往回拉三十秒，重看。

然後你躺回去，維持同一個一定會再出事的姿勢，繼續。

隔天你脖子轉不太過去，鼻樑上有一小塊紅。

同事問你怎麼了。

你總不能說：我被自己的追劇進度打了一巴掌。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個躺著看劇被手機砸過臉、隔天落枕還嘴硬的人；配「昨天不小心撞到」的自拍效果最好
variations: 延伸版：躺著追劇的姿勢演化史——仰躺舉手、側躺歪頭、把手機靠在枕頭上、最後直接架在肚子上，用一個下巴貼胸口的角度看完最後兩集。
反轉版：真正的高手會買一支床邊手機支架，然後在第三天發現自己躺得更遠、看得更久、睡得更晚——工具沒有救你，它只是把你的極限往後推了兩集。

en.content:
Anyone who watches shows lying down has had that moment.

Arm straight up over your face, holding steady for twenty minutes, until it starts going numb.
You roll onto your side. The picture is tilted, so you tilt your head to match. Now you're both crooked.

Then your eyelids go slack for half a second —

and the phone lands face-first on the bridge of your nose.

It hurts enough to sit you straight up, and your first move isn't to rub your nose.
It's to check the screen: how much did I miss.

Back up thirty seconds. Rewatch.

Then you lie down again, in the exact position guaranteed to do it again, and keep going.

The next day your neck won't turn all the way and there's a small red mark on your nose.

A coworker asks what happened.

And you can't exactly say: my own watch progress slapped me in the face.
en.editorNote: For the person whose phone has fallen on their face mid-episode and who blamed the crick in their neck on "sleeping funny"; pairs perfectly with a "totally just bumped into something" selfie
variations: Extended: the evolution of lying-down watching — arm overhead, head tilted sideways, phone propped on a pillow, and finally balanced on your stomach so you finish the last two episodes with your chin welded to your chest.

Reversal: the enlightened move is buying a bedside phone mount, and then discovering on day three that you now lie further back, watch longer, and sleep later — the gadget didn't save you, it just pushed your limit out by two more episodes.

items.sourceNote: 串流介面操作體驗研究，原創改編為電視遙控器逐格打字搜尋的挫折情境

zh-tw.content:
用電視搜尋一部劇，是一種現代酷刑。

螢幕上排著一整面的字，游標一格一格移。
你只是想打四個字，游標走了三十七步。

打到第三個字你按錯，刪除鍵在最右邊，於是游標又要一路走回去。

這時候電視非常貼心地跳出推薦：
八部跟你要找的完全無關的劇。

你放棄了。

你拿起手機，三秒打完，投到電視上。

那台號稱智慧的電視，此刻唯一的功能，是一面很貴的螢幕。

而你手上那支六吋的東西，才是你真正的遙控器、鍵盤、搜尋引擎和決策中心。

科技進步了這麼多年，最後的標準解法還是：
手機打字，電視放大。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個在客廳用遙控器一格一格選字、最後還是掏出手機投放的人；也適合當智慧電視受害者互助會開場白
variations: 延伸版：所以家裡的分工其實很清楚——電視負責大，手機負責聰明，而你負責在兩者之間來回，扮演一條會走路的傳輸線。
反轉版：真正的絕望是你投放成功、畫面出來了，然後全家安靜三秒，有人說：「這部我們上個月看過了。」

en.content:
Searching for a show on a TV is a modern form of torture.

A full grid of letters on screen, and a cursor that moves one square at a time.
You want to type four words. The cursor travels thirty-seven steps.

Halfway through you hit the wrong letter. Delete is parked in the far corner, so the cursor walks all the way back.

At which point the TV helpfully offers suggestions:
eight shows with nothing to do with what you typed.

You give up.

You pick up your phone, type it in three seconds, and cast it to the screen.

That allegedly smart television is, at this exact moment, functioning as an expensive rectangle.

And the six-inch thing in your hand is your actual remote, keyboard, search engine, and decision-making center.

After all these years of progress, the standard solution is still:
type on the phone, watch on the TV.
en.editorNote: For the person who spelled out a title one arrow-key at a time before giving up and casting from their phone; a solid opener for any smart-TV support group
variations: Extended: so the division of labor at home is actually very clear — the TV is big, the phone is smart, and you are the walking cable that carries things between them.
Reversal: true despair is landing the cast, watching it come up on the big screen, and then getting three seconds of family silence before someone says: "we watched this one last month."

items.sourceNote: 2026 串流疲勞調查：漲價促使觀眾改用含廣告方案、逾七成認為廣告過多，原創改編為廣告插點與時間成本的自嘲

zh-tw.content:
你降級成含廣告方案的那個月，每個月省下九十塊。

前兩集你覺得還好。廣告就三十秒，忍一下。

到第五集你發現一件事：廣告不是隨機插的。

它專挑那種——有人正要說出那句話、手已經舉起來、配樂剛剛推上去的時候。

黑屏。然後是一支洗衣精。

你已經會背那支洗衣精的台詞了。你甚至知道那個媽媽笑到第幾秒會轉頭。

一季看完，你對主角一家的關係還有點模糊，但你對那個洗衣精品牌有一種近乎親人的熟悉。

最後你算了一筆帳：
一季十六集，每集三段，每段九十秒。
你為了省九十塊，坐著多看了七十二分鐘。

你的時間被標了一個價格，
而且是你自己標的。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個為了省訂閱費改辦含廣告方案、現在會背每一支廣告台詞的人；也適合貼在「這插點絕對是故意的吧」的討論串
variations: 延伸版：更微妙的是廣告跑的那三十秒，你其實不會滑手機——你會盯著它看完，因為你怕錯過劇接回來的那一秒。連廣告都被你認真看完了。
反轉版：後來你升回無廣告方案，開播第一集，那支熟悉的洗衣精沒有出現，你居然愣了半秒——原來連被打斷這件事，都會養成習慣。

en.content:
The month you downgraded to the ad tier, you saved three dollars.

The first two episodes felt fine. Thirty seconds of ads. You can handle that.

By episode five you notice something: the ads are not placed at random.

They go looking for the exact moment someone is about to say the line, hand already raised, score already swelling.

Cut to black. Then laundry detergent.

You can recite that detergent spot from memory. You know precisely which second the mom turns her head.

By the end of the season you're still a little fuzzy on how the main family is related, but you have an almost familial closeness with a detergent brand.

Eventually you do the math:
sixteen episodes, three breaks each, ninety seconds a break.
To save three dollars, you sat through seventy-two extra minutes.

Your time now has a price on it,
and you're the one who set it.
en.editorNote: For the person who dropped to the ad-supported plan to save a few bucks and can now recite every commercial; also good in any "that ad break was placed on purpose" thread
variations: Extended: the strange part is you don't even scroll your phone during those thirty seconds — you watch the ad all the way through, because you're afraid of missing the second the show comes back.

Reversal: months later you upgrade back to ad-free, hit play on episode one, and the familiar detergent doesn't show up — and you pause for half a second. Turns out even being interrupted becomes a habit.

items.sourceNote: 追劇行為統計彙整，原創改編為「按暫停定格在最不上相的一格」的觀看細節

zh-tw.content:
追劇的人都知道一件事：你按暫停的那一格，通常很醜。

你只是要去倒杯水。手指一按，畫面停住。

回來的時候，全劇最好看的那個人，臉停在一個他這輩子都不想被看到的瞬間——

眼睛半閉，嘴巴張到一半，下巴的角度非常誠實。

你先笑了三秒。

然後你做了一件很奇怪的事：你往回拉一秒，再按一次暫停，想幫他找一個體面一點的畫面。

失敗。往前一格更慘。

你來回試了五次，像在幫一個不在場的人挑證件照。

最後你放棄，直接按播放。

那張臉一動起來，又變回那個讓你追了十二集的人。

你才想通：好看從來不是某一格。

是他動起來的樣子，是講那句台詞的節奏，是轉頭前那半秒的停頓。

拆開來看，誰都撐不住。

人也是。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個按暫停會定格在主角最不上相一格、還要來回幫他找體面畫面的人；也適合配上你手機裡那張捨不得刪的截圖
variations: 延伸版：所以真正的粉絲截圖是一門手藝——連按三次、挑最順的那一格、把字幕裁掉，發出去的時候還要假裝是隨手截的。
反轉版：更好笑的是那張醜圖你根本捨不得刪，後來還設成了追劇群組的封面；你喜歡的其實不是他最好看的樣子，是他最沒有防備的樣子。

en.content:
Everyone who watches shows knows this: the frame you pause on is almost always unflattering.

You just wanted a glass of water. One tap, and the picture freezes.

When you come back, the most beautiful person on the show is stuck in an expression he would not want preserved anywhere —

eyes half shut, mouth half open, jaw at an angle that is being extremely honest.

You laugh for three seconds.

Then you do something genuinely odd: you rewind one second and pause again, trying to find him a more dignified frame.

Failure. The next one is worse.

You try five times, like you're picking a passport photo for someone who isn't in the room.

Eventually you give up and hit play.

The face starts moving, and it turns back into the person you've watched twelve episodes for.

And it lands: attractiveness was never one frame.

It's the way he moves, the rhythm he gives that line, the half-second pause before he turns his head.

Broken into stills, nobody survives.

Neither do the rest of us.
en.editorNote: For the person who always pauses on the lead's worst frame and then hunts for a dignified one; pairs well with that screenshot you can't bring yourself to delete
variations: Extended: which is why fan screenshots are a craft — tap three times, pick the cleanest frame, crop out the subtitles, then post it like you grabbed it without thinking.
Reversal: the funny part is you never delete the ugly one. It ends up as the group chat's cover image. What you liked was never his best angle — it was the one where he wasn't guarding anything.

items.sourceNote: 影集總時數計算工具（集數乘以片長換算天數）的使用情境，原創改編為開追長壽劇前的時數自我談判

zh-tw.content:
你查到那部劇有八季。

一百七十二集，每集四十五分鐘。

你打開計算機，按了一串數字，得到一個你不太想看的答案：

一百二十九個小時。

換算下來，是五天四夜完全不睡，或者每天一小時、看四個月。

你把手機放下，很認真地思考了一下人生。

四個月。四個月你可以把一種樂器學到入門，可以把陽台那盆快死的植物救回來，可以把床頭放了三年的書看完。

你想了大概九十秒。

然後你按了播放。

片頭跑出來的時候，你心裡冒出那句經典的自我談判：
「先看第一集，不喜歡就不看了。」

你當然會喜歡。

計算機算得出來的是時數，算不出來的是——
你其實不是在花掉一百二十九個小時，
你是在替接下來的四個月，先安排好一個每天願意早點回家的理由。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個開追長壽劇前一定先算總時數、算完照樣按播放的人；也適合回覆群組裡那句「這部有八季欸你確定？」
variations: 延伸版：追劇族的時間感很特別——三十分鐘就能做完的雜事會拖一整週，一百二十九個小時的劇兩週就沒了。時間從來不是不夠，它只是只肯往你真的想去的地方流。
反轉版：真正的分水嶺在第三季某一集，你發現自己不再算還剩幾集，而是開始害怕它會播完——那一刻你就從觀眾變成家人了。

en.content:
You look it up. The show has eight seasons.

One hundred seventy-two episodes, forty-five minutes each.

You open the calculator, punch in the numbers, and get an answer you'd rather not have:

One hundred twenty-nine hours.

That's five straight days without sleeping, or four months at an hour a night.

You put the phone down and seriously reflect on your life.

Four months. In four months you could get decent at an instrument, revive the half-dead plant on the balcony, finish the book that's been on your nightstand for three years.

You consider this for roughly ninety seconds.

Then you hit play.

As the opening titles roll, the classic negotiation surfaces:
"I'll just watch the first episode, and if I don't like it I'll stop."

Of course you'll like it.

The calculator can total the hours. What it can't total is this —
you aren't spending a hundred twenty-nine hours,
you're arranging, in advance, a reason to want to be home early for the next four months.
en.editorNote: For the person who calculates the total runtime before starting a long series and presses play anyway; also a good reply to "eight seasons, are you sure about this?"
variations: Extended: bingers have a strange sense of time — a thirty-minute errand can stretch across a whole week, while a hundred-plus-hour show disappears in two. Time was never short; it just only flows toward where you actually want to be.

Reversal: the real turning point is somewhere in season three, when you stop counting how many episodes are left and start dreading that it ends. That's the moment you stop being a viewer and start being family.

items.sourceNote: 貓為何窩在飼主腿上（想靠近、視野好）的行為解析，原創改編為貓壓住腿導致自動播放連追數集的追劇情境

zh-tw.content:
沙發上追劇的人，有一條不成文的法律：
貓睡在你腿上的時候，你不能動。

牠是在第二集中間跳上來的。原地轉了三圈，找到一個牠滿意的角度，然後把整個重量放下去。

從那一秒開始，你的下半身就不歸你管了。

你想去廁所。不行。
你想拿桌上那杯已經涼掉的水。不行，那要伸手，伸手會牽動大腿。
遙控器在一公尺外，等於在另一個縣市。

所以你什麼都沒做，讓它自動播放——那是唯一不需要移動的選項。

第三集、第四集、第五集。

你的腳麻了，膀胱在抗議，肩膀因為維持同一個姿勢開始發酸。

而牠睡得很沉，偶爾抽動一下鬍鬚。

十二點多，牠終於伸個懶腰跳下去，頭也不回地走了。

你重獲自由的第一件事，不是站起來。

是先看一眼進度：喔，第六集了。

你不是自己想追那麼多集。

你只是被留在原地，而剛好有東西陪你把那三個小時走完。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個貓一睡上腿就整個人定住、只好一路自動播放到第六集的人；貓奴追劇群組的認領文
variations: 延伸版：另一種版本是牠直接坐在螢幕正前方，尾巴不偏不倚掃過主角的臉——你不會叫牠走，你會把身體歪過去遷就牠，用一個很奇怪的角度看完那場戲。
反轉版：更慘的是牠跳下去之後，腿上那塊還是溫的，你居然有點捨不得動；最後你又坐了二十分鐘，跟自己說是為了看完這一集。

en.content:
There's an unwritten law for people who watch shows on the couch:
when the cat is asleep on your legs, you do not move.

She jumped up midway through episode two. Turned three circles, found an angle she approved of, and set her full weight down.

From that second on, the lower half of your body was no longer yours.

You need the bathroom. Denied.
You want the glass of water that went cold on the table. Denied — that requires reaching, and reaching moves your thigh.
The remote is three feet away, which is to say, in another county.

So you do nothing and let it autoplay. It's the only option that requires no movement.

Episode three. Four. Five.

Your foot has gone numb, your bladder is filing complaints, your shoulder aches from holding one position.

She sleeps deeply, whiskers twitching now and then.

A little after midnight she finally stretches, hops down, and leaves without looking back.

The first thing you do with your freedom is not stand up.

It's check the progress: oh. Episode six.

You didn't actually mean to watch that many.

You were just held in place, and something happened to keep you company for those three hours.
en.editorNote: For the person who freezes the instant the cat lands on their lap and autoplays all the way to episode six; instantly claimed by every cat owner in the group chat
variations: Extended: the other version is when she sits directly in front of the screen, tail sweeping precisely across the lead's face — and you don't move her. You lean sideways to accommodate her and finish the scene at a deeply strange angle.
Reversal: worse is after she leaves and the spot on your leg is still warm, and you don't want to disturb it. You sit there another twenty minutes, telling yourself it's just to finish the episode.

items.sourceNote: 維基百科「期待（情緒）」條目關於預期本身即帶來報酬的說明，原創改編為連假還很遠就先排好片表的心理

zh-tw.content:
週日晚上十一點，你不在看劇。

你在做一張表。

窗外還是夏天的溫度，你已經在想九月底。

中秋那天是週五，後面那個週一也放假，中間夾著一個週末——你數了三次，確定是四天。

於是你打開備忘錄，開始排：第一天下午開那部你一直不敢開的長劇；第二天配著午餐看輕鬆的；第三天留給重看；第四天不排，因為要留一格給「看不完的那部」。

你排得比公司的專案還細。

排完你看著那張表，心裡有一種很奇怪的滿足感——那四天還沒到，你已經先過了一遍。

然後你關掉備忘錄。明天早上七點的鬧鐘還在那裡。

你知道這張表最後大概不會照著跑。上次你也排過，結果四天裡有三天在睡。

但那不重要。

因為這張表的功能從來不是拿來執行的。

它的功能是讓你在一個什麼都還沒發生的週日晚上，
先確認前面有一件確定會很快樂的事，
然後你就可以安心地，
把中間那一串日子，一天一天走過去。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個八月就把中秋那四天要看什麼排好的人；也適合回覆群組裡那句「離連假還有多久」
variations: 延伸版：真正的追劇族排連假不是排劇，是排復原時間——最後半天一定留白，因為你知道自己需要一段從別人的故事走回自己生活的緩衝。
反轉版：連假結束那天你回頭看那張表，只打勾了一項，卻一點都不失望——最好的那部分，你早在寫表的那個晚上就先拿走了。

en.content:
Mid-Autumn is seven weeks out and you're already building the schedule.

It's eleven at night, a Sunday in August. The air outside still feels like summer and you are thinking about late September.

The holiday lands on a Friday. The Monday after it is a day off too. With the weekend in the middle, you count three times to be sure: four days.

So you open the notes app and start assigning. Day one, afternoon: the long series you've been afraid to start. Day two: something light, over lunch. Day three: a rewatch. Day four stays blank, because you need one slot for whatever you didn't finish.

You plan it in more detail than anything at work.

Then you look at the list and feel something oddly close to satisfaction. Those four days haven't happened yet and you've already lived through them once.

You close the app. The 7 a.m. alarm is still set.

You know the list won't survive contact with reality. Last time you made one, you slept through three of the four days.

Doesn't matter.

The list was never meant to be executed.

It exists so that on an ordinary Sunday night when nothing has happened yet,
you can confirm there's a good thing waiting up ahead,
and then walk through everything between here and there, one day at a time.
en.editorNote: For the person who has the Mid-Autumn long weekend fully programmed before August is over; also a good reply to "how long until the break?"
variations: Extended: seasoned bingers don't schedule shows, they schedule recovery — the last half-day always stays blank, because you know you need a buffer to walk back from someone else's story into your own life.
Reversal: on the final day of the break you look at the list and exactly one box is checked, and you aren't disappointed. You took the best part of it weeks earlier, on the night you wrote it.

items.sourceNote: 維基百科敘事傳輸理論條目關於觀眾投入故事後的殘留效應，原創改編為追完劇隔天出門那三十秒的「主角感」

zh-tw.content:
追完一部好劇的隔天早上，你會有大概三十秒的主角感。

你出門買早餐，戴上耳機，剛好放到那首你聽了三十集的曲子。

你的走路速度自動慢了半拍。

你沒有低頭滑手機，你抬頭看了一下天空，那個角度很像某一場戲的開場鏡頭。

經過巷口那家早餐店，你覺得老闆娘跟你打招呼的樣子都有點溫柔。

主角感就是這種東西：它不會讓你變帥，也不會讓你變勇敢，它只是讓你在很短的時間裡，覺得自己這條普通的路上有鏡頭。

然後你走到路口，紅燈。一台機車從旁邊擠過去，後照鏡差點勾到你的袖子。

主角感結束。

你把音量調小，繼續往前走。

但奇怪的是，那天你做了一件拖了兩個月的事。

你不知道為什麼，你只知道那個早上你比較敢。

主角感沒什麼用，它只是借你一點膽子，
而且很短，
短到你只來得及拿它做一件事——
所以下次它來的時候，記得挑一件重要的。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個追完劇隔天走路特別慢、還自己配好片頭曲的朋友；也適合當作「今天要把那件拖很久的事做掉」的開場白
variations: 延伸版：主角感有便宜的版本——下雨天戴上耳機，隨便一首歌都會讓你覺得這段路值得被拍下來。
反轉版：追久了你會發現，最好的劇給你的不是主角感，是配角感——你開始注意到那些只出現兩場戲的人，也開始相信自己在別人的故事裡，也算某一種角色。

en.content:
Main-character energy has a shelf life of about thirty seconds.

The morning after you finish a great show, you head out for breakfast, put your headphones in, and the song you've heard thirty times comes on.

Your walking speed drops half a beat.

You don't look down at your phone. You look up at the sky, at an angle that could open an episode.

You pass the breakfast place on the corner and the owner's nod seems, somehow, tender.

That's all it is. It doesn't make you better looking or braver. It just makes you feel, briefly, that there's a camera on this very ordinary street.

Then you reach the crosswalk. Red light. A scooter squeezes past and its mirror nearly catches your sleeve.

End of scene.

You turn the volume down and keep walking.

The strange part: that day you did a thing you'd been putting off for two months.

You don't know why. You only know you were braver that morning.

It's useless, that feeling. It just lends you a little nerve,
and not for long —
only long enough for one thing.
So next time it shows up, pick something that matters.
en.editorNote: For the friend who walks noticeably slower the morning after finishing a series, scoring the sidewalk with the show's theme; also the nudge for finally doing the thing you keep postponing
variations: Extended: there's a budget version — headphones plus rain, and any song at all will convince you this walk deserves to be filmed.

Reversal: watch enough shows and you notice the best ones don't hand you main-character energy, they hand you supporting-character energy — you start seeing the people who get two scenes, and start believing you count as somebody in someone else's story too.

items.sourceNote: 維基百科蔡加尼克效應（未完成的事更容易被記住）條目，原創改編為三年來進度永遠停在同一集的那部劇

zh-tw.content:
有一部劇，你跟它的關係卡在第四集，卡了三年。

你不是討厭它。每次有人提到，你都說：「那部很好看，我一定會看完。」

三年來你打開過四次。

第一次是剛加進清單，看了三集，很喜歡，然後那週你搬家。
第二次是隔年冬天，從第一集重看，看到第四集，睡著。
第三次你直接跳到第四集，撐了二十分鐘，發現前面全忘了，關掉。
第四次是上個月，你點開，看到進度停在第四集第十八分鐘，你盯著它三秒，然後去看了別的。

每個人的清單裡都有這樣一部。

它不難看，也沒有得罪你。

它只是每次出現的時候，都剛好碰上你比較滿的那段日子——你那時候需要的是可以分心看的東西，而它需要你專心。

有些劇不是你不看，是你跟它一直對不上時間。

它會一直停在那裡，第四集第十八分鐘，等一個你剛好有空、又剛好想安靜下來的晚上。

那天會來的。
可能不是今年。
但你們還沒結束。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個講了三年「我一定會看完」、進度永遠停在第四集的朋友；也適合安撫自己那份看了會心虛的待看清單
variations: 延伸版：更玄的是你每次都在同一個場景睡著，那一段像一道門，你連續三年沒走過去。
反轉版：真的有一天你把它看完了，會發現它比記憶中更好看，然後有點生氣——氣自己讓一件確定會喜歡的事，在原地等了三年。

en.content:
Episode four is where you and that show have been stuck for three years.

You don't dislike it. Whenever it comes up you say, "That one's great, I'll definitely finish it."

In three years you've opened it four times.

First time: three episodes in, loving it, and then you moved apartments that week.
Second time: the following winter, restarting from episode one, asleep by four.
Third time: you skipped straight to four, lasted twenty minutes, realized you'd forgotten everything before it, and quit.
Fourth time: last month. You opened it, saw the bar parked at episode four, eighteen minutes in, stared for three seconds, and watched something else.

Everyone has one of these.

It isn't bad. It never did anything to you.

It just keeps arriving during your fuller stretches — the months when you need something you can half-watch, and it needs you all the way there.

Some shows go unwatched not because you don't want them, but because you and the timing keep missing each other.

It'll stay exactly where it is, episode four, eighteen minutes, waiting for a night when you happen to be free and happen to want quiet.

That night will come.
Maybe not this year.
The two of you aren't finished.
en.editorNote: For the friend who's been saying "I'll definitely finish it" for three years with the progress bar frozen at episode four; also for making peace with your own guilty watchlist
variations: Extended: the eerie part is falling asleep at the same scene every single time — that stretch is a door you haven't managed to walk through in three years.
Reversal: the day you finally finish it, it's better than you remembered, and that irritates you — you left something you were guaranteed to love sitting in a corner for three years.

items.sourceNote: 維基百科決策疲勞條目關於夜間決策品質下降的說明，原創改編為深夜挑劇時只看每集片長的篩選行為

zh-tw.content:
晚上十一點四十，你在挑今晚要看什麼。

你點開一部劇的簡介，眼睛完全沒在讀劇情，直接找那個數字：每集 58 分鐘。

太長。返回。

下一部：42 分鐘。可以。

再下一部：73 分鐘。你笑了一聲，好像它侮辱了你。

年輕的時候你選劇看題材、看評價、看誰演的。

現在你選劇的第一個條件，是它能不能在你睡著之前結束。

42 分鐘是一種很奇妙的長度：剛好夠一個故事往前推，也剛好短到讓你可以跟自己說「看完這集就去刷牙」。

當然你不會只看一集。

但那不是重點。

重點是你在按下播放之前，做了一次很誠實的計算——不是算這部劇有多長，是算你今天還剩下多少。

成年人的娛樂是有額度的。

你不是變挑了，
你只是終於學會在打開一個故事以前，
先看一眼自己還剩幾分鐘。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個點開簡介先看片長、超過一小時就默默返回的人；也適合半夜十一點半還卡在片單前面的自己
variations: 延伸版：同一套標準會外溢到別的地方——超過三十分鐘的會議、要走十五分鐘的餐廳、需要換兩次車的邀約。你不是懶，你是在管理一天剩下的那點電。
反轉版：真正好看的劇會讓這套標準當場失效——點開時看到 71 分鐘你皺了一下眉，看完的第一個反應卻是：「這麼快就沒了？」

en.content:
Runtime is the first number you look for now — before the plot, before the cast.

It's 11:40 p.m. and you're picking tonight's show.

You open a description and your eyes skip everything to find the digits: 58 minutes per episode.

Too long. Back.

Next one: 42 minutes. Acceptable.

Next: 73 minutes. You actually laugh, like it insulted you.

Younger you chose by genre, by reviews, by who was in it.

Now the first criterion is whether it can finish before you do.

Forty-two minutes is a remarkable length: long enough for a story to move, short enough that you can tell yourself you'll brush your teeth right after.

You won't stop at one, obviously.

Not the point.

The point is that before pressing play, you ran an honest calculation — not how long the show is, but how much of today you have left.

Grown-up leisure runs on a quota.

You didn't get pickier.
You just finally learned to check, before opening a story,
how many minutes of yourself are still in the account.
en.editorNote: For the person who checks episode length first and silently backs out of anything over an hour; also for yourself, stalled in front of the watchlist at half past eleven
variations: Extended: the same rule leaks into everything else — meetings over thirty minutes, restaurants fifteen minutes away, invitations that require two transfers. Not laziness. Battery management.
Reversal: a genuinely great show voids the rule on contact — you frown at the 71 minutes going in, and coming out your first thought is "that's it? already?"

items.sourceNote: 維基百科動態範圍壓縮條目關於對白與音效音量落差、夜間模式的說明，原創改編為整晚右手黏在音量鍵上的追劇情境

zh-tw.content:
「他剛剛說什麼？」

你倒退十秒。還是聽不清楚。

於是你把音量從 12 轉到 20。這次聽見了：那句話很重要，是關於他哥哥。

三十秒後，車子爆炸。

你整個人從沙發上彈起來，手掌拍在遙控器上把音量砍到 6，同時抬頭看牆壁——隔壁有沒有被吵醒。

從那一刻開始，你的右手就沒有離開過音量鍵。

兩個人坐著講話：＋8。
配樂進來：－6。
開始吵架：＋4。
下雨的空景：－3。

你不是在追劇，你是在當混音師，還是那種沒有加班費的。

最後你放棄了，把字幕打開。

聽得懂的語言，你還是開了字幕——因為那是整部劇裡唯一不會忽大忽小的東西。

有人跟你解釋，那叫動態範圍，是為電影院的音響設計的，你家那兩顆藏在螢幕背面的喇叭放不出來。

你點點頭，稍微被安慰到。

但真正的問題你心裡清楚：
你家不是電影院，
你只是一個晚上十一點半、不想吵到任何人、
卻很想聽清楚那句台詞的人。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個左手抓零食、右手整晚黏在音量鍵上的人；也適合半夜被爆炸聲嚇到、立刻抬頭看牆壁的自己
variations: 延伸版：同一條曲線在別的地方也成立——預告片一開就把音量炸開、廣告比正片大聲、下一集的片頭曲比所有對白都響。你家遙控器上磨得最白的按鍵，不是電源鍵。
反轉版：偶爾會有一場戲讓你自己主動把音量調大——沒有配樂、沒有台詞，只有兩個人坐著不說話。你不是要聽清楚什麼，你是想把那個沉默聽得更仔細一點。

en.content:
"What did he just say?"

You skip back ten seconds. Still can't make it out.

So you take the volume from 12 to 20. Now you hear it: the line matters, it's about his brother.

Thirty seconds later, a car explodes.

You come off the couch, slam your palm on the remote until it reads 6, and look at the wall — checking whether the neighbors are awake.

From that moment your right hand never leaves the volume button again.

Two people talking: +8.
Score comes in: -6.
Argument starts: +4.
Slow shot of rain: -3.

You're not watching a show. You're mixing one, unpaid, in real time.

Eventually you give up and turn on the subtitles.

A language you understand perfectly, and you turn on subtitles anyway — because they're the one element of the whole production that stays the same size.

Someone explains that this is dynamic range, mixed for theater systems, and the two speakers hidden behind your screen were never going to reproduce it.

You nod. It helps a little.

But you know what the actual problem is:
your living room is not a theater,
and you're just a person at 11:30 at night
who doesn't want to wake anyone and would very much like to hear that one line.
en.editorNote: For the person with snacks in the left hand and a thumb welded to the volume button all evening; also for yourself, jolted by an explosion and immediately checking the wall
variations: Extended: the same curve shows up everywhere else — trailers that open at full blast, ads louder than the show, a theme song that outguns every line of dialogue in the episode. The most worn-down button on your remote is not the power button.

Reversal: once in a while a scene makes you turn it up on purpose — no score, no dialogue, two people sitting there not speaking. You're not straining to hear anything. You just want to hear the silence more closely.

items.sourceNote: Psychology Today 關於手機提示音形成制約反應、刺激類化的討論，原創改編為劇中鈴聲響起卻先摸自己口袋的追劇情境

zh-tw.content:
劇裡的手機響了。

你摸了自己的口袋。

明明那個鈴聲不是你的，明明螢幕上就有一支手機在桌上震動，明明女主角已經接起來了——你的手還是先動了。

更慘的是通知音。

那種短短的「叮」，跟你設定的一模一樣。

你低頭、解鎖、滑開。什麼都沒有。抬起頭，劇已經演過三句台詞。

於是你倒回去重看，然後在同一集裡，被同一種聲音騙第二次。

你不是笨。

你只是被訓練了很多年：那個聲音出現，就代表有人找你、有事發生、有東西該看。

心理學把這個叫制約，就是那個聽到鈴聲會流口水的實驗。

差別只在於，狗至少每次都有東西吃。

你有的是一個空的鎖定畫面，
和一段要重看的劇情。

最好笑的版本是——
那一次劇裡根本沒有響。

是你自己以為它響了。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個劇裡電話一響就摸自己口袋的人；分心追劇群組的認領文，也適合貼在自己那支永遠沒有新訊息的手機旁邊
variations: 延伸版：反過來也會發生。你自己的手機真的響了，你以為是劇裡的，等到第三聲才回過神，接起來已經進語音信箱。你回撥過去，對方說「沒事了」。
反轉版：有一部劇你看到後面，連男主角的鈴聲都聽熟了。某天在捷運上有人的手機這樣響，你整個人回頭——在人群裡找一個不存在的角色。

en.content:
A phone rings in the show.

You pat your own pocket.

The ringtone isn't yours. There is a phone visibly buzzing on a table onscreen. The lead has already picked it up. Your hand moved anyway.

Notification sounds are worse.

That short bright chime, identical to the one you use.

You look down, unlock, swipe. Nothing. You look up and three lines of dialogue have gone by.

So you skip back — and get fooled by the same sound a second time, in the same episode.

You're not slow.

You've just been trained for years: that sound means someone wants you, something happened, something needs looking at.

Psychology calls it conditioning. It's the experiment with the bell and the dog.

The difference being that the dog got fed every time.

You get an empty lock screen
and thirty seconds of plot to rewatch.

The funniest version is the night
nothing rang in the show at all.

You just thought it did.
en.editorNote: For the person who pats their pocket every time a phone rings onscreen; instantly claimed by the group chat, and worth taping to your own permanently message-free phone
variations: Extended: it runs the other way too. Your phone actually rings, you assume it belongs to the show, and by the third ring it's gone to voicemail. You call back and they say never mind.

Reversal: deep into one series you know the lead's ringtone by heart. Weeks later a stranger's phone goes off with it on the train and you turn around — scanning a crowd for a person who doesn't exist.

items.sourceNote: Netflix 技術部落格關於封面圖個人化、從數百張候選截圖挑選並持續測試的說明，原創改編為同一部劇每天換一張臉的首頁體驗

zh-tw.content:
首頁最上面那部劇，你昨天明明滑過去了。

今天它換了一張臉。

昨天的封面是兩個人站在雨裡，看起來像愛情片，你沒興趣。
今天的封面是一個人拿著刀站在長廊上，看起來很懸疑，你點了進去。

點進去發現：就是昨天那部。

第三天它又變了，這次圖上是一隻狗。

你開始懷疑這部劇到底在演什麼。

它什麼都演。平台只是從幾百張截圖裡，挑一張它覺得你會點的給你。

你在誰的臉上停比較久、你對哪種顏色反應比較大、你上禮拜看完了什麼——它都算過。

所以你跟朋友看到的同一部劇，長得不一樣。你們花了十分鐘討論「封面是黑白的那部」，最後發現講的是同一部。

讓人有點涼的是這件事：

決定你今晚看什麼的，可能不是劇本、不是演員、不是評價。

是一張系統認為你會點的圖。

你以為你在挑劇。

比較準確的說法是：
有人非常認真地研究過，什麼樣的一張圖會把你騙進來，
而且研究了很久——久到比你了解自己還久。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個「這部我怎麼沒看過」點進去發現早就看過的人；也適合跟朋友對不上同一部劇封面的時候丟出來
variations: 延伸版：你可以自己驗證。用別人的帳號登進同一個平台，翻到同一部劇，封面通常不一樣。那不是 bug，那是一份關於你們兩個人的報告。
反轉版：它也有失手的時候。連續五天換了五張圖想把同一部推給你，你每次都滑過去。第六天它放棄了，那部劇從你的首頁消失。你當下鬆了一口氣，兩個禮拜後卻突然想起來：那部到底叫什麼？

en.content:
That show at the top of your homepage — you scrolled past it yesterday.

Today it has a different face.

Yesterday the image was two people standing in the rain. Looked like a romance. Not interested.
Today it's one person holding a knife at the end of a corridor. Looks tense. You click.

It's yesterday's show.

On day three it changes again. This time there's a dog on it.

You start to wonder what this show is actually about.

It's about all of it. The platform simply picks, from hundreds of candidate frames, the one it thinks you'll click.

Whose face you linger on, which colors get a reaction out of you, what you finished last week — all of it went into that choice.

Which is why the show you're looking at doesn't match the show your friend is looking at. You spend ten minutes discussing "the one with the black-and-white poster" before realizing you mean the same series.

The genuinely unsettling part:

what decides your evening may not be the writing, or the cast, or the reviews.

It's one still frame a system believes will work on you.

You think you're choosing a show.

More accurately:
someone studied, very carefully, which single image gets you through the door —
and they've been studying it longer than you've been paying attention to yourself.
en.editorNote: For the person who clicks something new and finds a show they already finished; also good for the moment you and a friend can't agree on what a series looks like
variations: Extended: you can test it. Open the same platform on someone else's account and find the same title. The artwork usually differs. That's not a bug — that's a report about the two of you.

Reversal: sometimes it misses. Five days, five different images for the same show, and you scroll past every one. On day six it gives up and the title disappears from your homepage. You feel relieved, and then two weeks later you think: wait, what was that one called?

items.sourceNote: 維基百科舌尖現象條目關於想不起名字卻記得其他細節的說明，原創改編為追劇時全程用外號稱呼角色的情境

zh-tw.content:
你追了三十集，還是不知道男主角叫什麼名字。

在你腦子裡，他們的名字長這樣：

穿黑外套的。
賣魚的那個。
一直咳嗽的伯伯。
妹妹的前男友。
第二集就很可疑的那個。

所以你跟朋友討論劇情，整段對話像在猜謎：

「所以賣魚的知道那件事了嗎？」
「哪個賣魚的？」
「就手上有疤的那個。」
「喔——他不是叫……算了，對，他知道了。」

十分鐘後，你們順利完成一場沒有出現任何一個名字的完整劇情討論。

奇怪的是，名字你記不住，
但他在第七集站在門口猶豫了兩秒才敲門，你記得。

他把傘留給誰、他吃飯的時候碗端多高、他生氣之前會先笑一下——你全部記得。

原來你從來就不是靠名字認人的。

你認的是動作、是習慣、是那一秒的表情。

現實生活也一樣。
你可能叫不出某個人的全名，
但你記得他講電話的時候會轉筆。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個整部劇都用「賣魚的那個」稱呼角色的人；也適合追劇群組裡開始猜謎時丟出來緩頰
variations: 延伸版：這套外號系統有嚴重的相容性問題。同一個角色，你叫他「賣魚的」，你朋友叫他「戴帽子那個」，你們認真吵了五分鐘，才發現講的是同一個人。
反轉版：真正投入的時候，名字會自己黏上來。有一部劇你連配角的表哥叫什麼都記得——而那個表哥全劇總共只出現兩次。

en.content:
Thirty episodes in and you still don't know the lead's name.

In your head, the cast list reads like this:

Black coat guy.
The one who sells fish.
The uncle who keeps coughing.
The sister's ex.
Obviously suspicious since episode two.

Which makes discussing the plot with a friend sound like a riddle contest:

"So does fish guy know yet?"
"Which fish guy?"
"The one with the scar on his hand."
"Oh — isn't his name… never mind. Yes. He knows."

Ten minutes later you've completed an entire detailed conversation about the show without either of you saying a single name.

The strange part: you can't hold onto the names,
but you remember him standing at the door in episode seven, hesitating two full seconds before he knocked.

Who he left the umbrella with. How high he holds a bowl when he eats. The small laugh that arrives right before he gets angry. All of it.

Turns out you were never identifying people by name.

You identify them by gesture, by habit, by one second of expression.

Same as real life.
You might blank on someone's full name
and still remember that they spin a pen while they're on the phone.
en.editorNote: For the person who spent an entire series calling someone "the fish guy"; good to drop in the group chat the moment plot discussion turns into a guessing game
variations: Extended: the nickname system has serious compatibility problems. You call him "fish guy," your friend calls him "the one in the hat," and you argue in earnest for five minutes before realizing it's the same man.
Reversal: when you're truly invested the names stick by themselves. There's one show where you know the name of a side character's cousin — a cousin who appears exactly twice.

items.sourceNote: TV Tropes 關係圖條目與觀眾為群像劇自製人物關係圖的討論，原創改編為半夜在紙上畫十九個名字的追劇情境

zh-tw.content:
追到第九集，你去拿了一張紙。

不是要記待辦事項，是要畫人物關係圖。

左上角寫男主角，右上角寫女主角，中間拉一條線。然後你發現不夠——他還有一個師兄、兩個表親、一個立場不明的下屬，女主角那邊還有一整個家族在排隊等著被畫進來。

紙翻面，重畫。這次你學聰明了：三個陣營分開，用不同顏色的筆。

畫到一半你停下來，因為出現了一個問題：那個人到底是誰的兒子？

你倒回第四集確認完，回來補了一條虛線，旁邊寫「疑似」。

畫完是凌晨十二點四十。桌上那張紙有十九個名字、二十六條線、四個問號。

你看著它，覺得有點好笑：

上個月開會前的資料，你只掃過標題。
上次要記家裡誰對什麼過敏，你還記錯。

但為了一部演完就沒了的戲，你做出了這輩子最完整的一份筆記。

後來那張紙夾在書裡，某天掉出來。

你已經想不起那些虛線在猶豫什麼了，

只記得那幾個晚上，你是真的很在乎。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個追群像劇要先畫圖才看得懂的人；也適合貼在自己那張畫到一半就停住的關係圖旁邊
variations: 延伸版：這種圖都有一個共同的命運——畫到第二十集就停了。不是你放棄，是你終於記起來了。真正認得一群人，從來不是靠圖，是靠他們吵過的架。
反轉版：也有白畫的時候。你把三個陣營分得漂漂亮亮，第三十集編劇讓其中兩邊和解，你辛苦分開的顏色一夜之間全部作廢。你盯著那張紙看了三秒，然後笑了——你其實很高興自己畫錯。

en.content:
Nine episodes in, you go get a piece of paper.

Not for a to-do list. For a character map.

One lead top left, the other top right, a line between them. Then you realize that won't hold — he has a mentor's son, two cousins, and a subordinate whose loyalties are unclear, and her side has an entire family queued up waiting to be drawn in.

Flip the page. Start over. This time you're smart about it: three factions, separated, different colored pens.

Halfway through you stop, because a question comes up. Whose son is that guy, exactly?

You skip back to episode four, confirm it, return and add a dashed line with "probably?" written beside it.

You finish at 12:40 in the morning. Nineteen names, twenty-six lines, four question marks.

You look at it and it's a little funny:

Last month you skimmed the headings of a deck before a meeting.
Last time you tried to recall who in your family is allergic to what, you got it wrong.

But for a show that ends and is gone, you produced the most thorough set of notes of your adult life.

The page ends up between the pages of a book. Months later it falls out.

You can't remember what those dashed lines were hesitating about anymore.

You just remember that for a few nights there, you genuinely cared.
en.editorNote: For the person who needs a hand-drawn chart to follow an ensemble drama; also good taped beside your own map that stalled halfway
variations: Extended: every one of these charts shares a fate — it stops around episode twenty. Not because you gave up, but because you finally know them. You never learn a cast from a diagram. You learn them from the fights they've had.

Reversal: sometimes it's wasted effort. You color-code the factions beautifully and then, in episode thirty, the writers have two of them make peace. Every careful separation you drew is void overnight. You stare at the page for three seconds, then laugh — you're glad you got it wrong.

items.sourceNote: 維基百科影視旅遊條目關於觀眾前往拍攝地朝聖的說明，原創改編為在劇中認出自家附近路口的情境

zh-tw.content:
第六集，男主角站在一個路口等紅燈。

你把畫面倒回去，又看了一次。

那是離你家走路七分鐘的地方。左邊那間你買過三次早餐，他背後那棟樓的磁磚缺了一角，你每天經過。

鏡頭裡它變得很好看。有霧、有光、有一段很慢的配樂，路口空得像整座城市只剩他一個人。

隔天早上你特地繞過去。

還是那個路口。垃圾車剛走，機車在等綠燈，早餐店照常在煎蛋，磁磚還是缺一角。

你站在他站過的位置，站了三十秒，什麼都沒發生。

過了幾週，你在網路上看到有人貼照片，說專程從很遠的地方飛過來，就為了站在這裡拍一張。留言底下一排人說羨慕。

你看著那張照片。那是你每天路過、從來沒抬頭看過的地方。

原來差別不在那個路口。

差別是有人願意在那裡站三十秒，

而你每天都是低著頭走過去的。
zh-tw.editorNote: 傳給那個在劇裡認出自家巷口的人；也適合在你嫌自己住的城市很無聊的那天翻出來看
variations: 延伸版：這件事有後遺症。從那天起你走路會偶爾停下來，把某個轉角當成一個鏡位——想像它有配樂、有慢動作。你不會跟任何人講，但那條路真的變得好走一點。
反轉版：也有失望的版本。你查到某部劇的拍攝地點，特地跑一趟，發現那間店收了，那面牆重新粉刷過。你拍了張照，跟劇裡完全不像。你把照片留著，覺得這樣也好——那個畫面只留在劇裡，就沒有人能再改它。

en.content:
Episode six. He's standing at an intersection, waiting for the light.

You skip back and watch it again.

That's a seven-minute walk from your apartment. You've bought breakfast at the place on the left three times. The building behind him is missing a corner tile. You pass it every day.

On camera it looks beautiful. There's haze, there's light, there's a very slow piece of music, and the intersection is empty enough that he seems to be the last person in the city.

The next morning you go out of your way to walk past it.
